sections.h: Hands, hearts and foods in Mark 7
sections.b: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem object that Jesus' disciples eat with "unclean" (literally "common") hands, without the rinsing that the tradition of the elders required (Mark 7:1–5). Mark explains the custom for Gentile readers: hand-washing, immersion after the market, and the immersing of cups and pots (Mark 7:3–4). Jesus answers with a riddle: nothing that enters a person from outside can make him unclean; what comes out of the heart does (Mark 7:15–23). Scholars disagree whether he set aside the Torah's purity system, ranked moral impurity above ritual impurity in the prophets' way, or defended the older biblical view against a newer Pharisaic idea that impurity passes into the body through food (Furstenberg). Mark's own comment, "With this he made all foods clean" (Mark 7:19), applies the teaching to his mixed church.

common: Jesus taught that impurity comes from the heart, not from food or unwashed hands.
uncommon: Jesus was defending the Torah's own view of purity against a Pharisaic innovation, not abolishing it (Furstenberg, Boyarin).

sections.b: Mark alone adds the comment that Jesus' teaching "made all foods clean" (Mark 7:19). Most interpreters read it as the Gospel writer telling Gentile believers that the laws of clean and unclean animals do not bind them, as Peter learned in Acts 10 and Paul taught in Romans 14. Daniel Boyarin reads the participle as describing digestion, which "purges" all food, and David Rudolph as concerning food made impure by contact, not forbidden kinds of animals. The Byzantine text and the KJV make it part of Jesus' saying, "purging all meats." Matthew leaves the comment out (Matthew 15:17–20). How the churches apply this is set out in the card at Matthew 15:11.

common: Mark 7:19 is the clearest Gospel statement that Christians are free from the food laws.
uncommon: Mark 7:19 is about digestion or contact impurity and says nothing against kosher food (Boyarin, Rudolph).

sections.b: Jesus answers the Pharisees' question about hand-washing with Isaiah's words, "Their worship of me is empty; / the teachings they teach are human commands" (Mark 7:7), and with a case: a Korban vow that left parents without support, letting a tradition cancel the command to honor father and mother (Mark 7:9–13). The tradition of the elders became the Oral Torah of rabbinic Judaism, and later rabbis agreed that vows harming parents could be released. Christians have used the passage in their own arguments over Scripture and church tradition; see the card at Matthew 15.

Mark keeps the Hebrew-Aramaic word Korban, "an offering," and explains it (Mark 7:11). Declaring property Korban made it like a gift to the Temple and forbidden to the person named. An ossuary lid from near Jerusalem uses the formula, and the Mishnah later allows such a vow to be undone when it harms one's father and mother (Mishnah Nedarim 9:1). Jesus treats the vow, used against parents, as a human rule cancelling God's command.

sections.h: The Syrophoenician woman and a Gentile crowd (Mark 7:24–8:10)
sections.b: After the dispute about purity, Mark takes Jesus into Gentile country. A Greek woman, Syrophoenician by birth, begs him to free her daughter. Jesus says the children must eat their fill "first" and the bread should not go to the little dogs; she answers that the little dogs eat the children's scraps, and her daughter is freed (Mark 7:24–30). Jesus then heals a deaf man in the Decapolis (Mark 7:31–37) and feeds four thousand, some of them "from far off" (Mark 8:1–10), a crowd many readers take to be mostly Gentile. The order is Israel first, then the nations, and the bread is more than enough for both.

common: The Syrophoenician woman shows that Jesus' mission reached beyond Israel.
uncommon: The woman changed Jesus' mind and widened his mission.

sections.b: Mark says Jesus went into the territory of Tyre and stayed in a house, hoping no one would know (Mark 7:24). There a Syrophoenician mother found him. Gerd Theissen notes that Tyre bought grain from Galilee and that "the children's bread" would have stung in a region where Galilean villagers felt rich Gentile cities took their food. Jesus' return "by way of Sidon" makes a long loop through Phoenician land (Mark 7:31).

Two of Mark's healings appear in no other Gospel. Jesus takes a deaf man aside, puts his fingers in his ears, spits, touches his tongue, groans and says "Ephphatha" (Mark 7:33–34); he leads a blind man out of Bethsaida, spits on his eyes and lays hands on him twice before he sees clearly (Mark 8:23–25). The deaf man's rare word for "speaking with difficulty" comes from Isaiah 35:6, and the crowd's cry repeats Isaiah 35:5–6. Mark sets these healings around the disciples' own deafness and blindness (Mark 8:18) and at the start of the road to Jerusalem, which ends with another blind man who follows Jesus (Mark 10:52).

Mark keeps Jesus' Aramaic command to the deaf man, "Ephphatha," and translates it, "Open up!" (Mark 7:34). It belongs with talitha koum (Mark 5:41), Korban (Mark 7:11), Abba (Mark 14:36) and Eloi (Mark 15:34): words of Jesus kept in his own language for Greek-speaking readers. By the late 300s the word had entered the baptismal rite (Ambrose, On the Mysteries).

sections.h: Four thousand fed and a boy set free (Mark 8:1–10; 9:14–29)
sections.b: Mark tells a second feeding, of four thousand with seven loaves, in the region where Jesus has just been among Gentiles (Mark 8:1–10). Jesus later asks the disciples to remember the twelve baskets and the seven (Mark 8:19–20). After the transfiguration, the disciples fail to free a boy from a speechless spirit; Jesus frees him after his father's cry, "I believe! Help me with my unbelief!", and tells the disciples that this kind comes out only by prayer (Mark 9:14–29). John's report of an outsider casting out demons in Jesus' name draws the answer, "Anyone who is not against us is on our side" (Mark 9:38–40).

sections.h: "You are the Messiah" and the secret (Mark 8:27–9:13)
sections.b: Peter's confession in Mark is the shortest: "You are the Messiah" (Mark 8:29). Jesus orders silence (Mark 8:30), teaches that the Son of Man must suffer (Mark 8:31), and rebukes Peter's objection as Satan's. On the mountain the silence is given a limit: until the Son of Man has risen from among the dead (Mark 9:9). William Wrede built his theory of the "messianic secret" on these verses; many scholars today see real caution by Jesus in them, sharpened by Mark's story, since the title could not be understood without the cross.

Mark's Peter names Jesus the Messiah (Mark 8:29) and in the next breath rebukes him for speaking of suffering, and Jesus, looking at all the disciples, calls him Satan (Mark 8:32–33). On the mountain Peter calls Jesus "Rabbi," offers to build three booths, and does not know what to say because he is terrified (Mark 9:5–6). Mark has no blessing of Peter and no "on this rock" (compare Matthew 16:17–19). The tradition that Mark wrote down Peter's preaching would make these frank scenes ones Peter told against himself.

common: Mark's unflattering picture of Peter suggests it comes from Peter's own preaching.

sections.b: After Peter's confession, Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer much, be thrown out by the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, be killed and rise after three days (Mark 8:31). The second prediction is shorter: the Son of Man is being handed over into human hands (Mark 9:31). Between them Jesus speaks of the Son of Man coming in his Father's glory with the holy angels (Mark 8:38), joining Daniel 7's heavenly figure to suffering. Each prediction is followed by misunderstanding and by teaching on what following him means.

Mark's is the earliest and least polished account. He mentions only the clothes, "whiter than any cloth-bleacher on earth could make them" (Mark 9:3); he names Elijah before Moses; Peter calls Jesus "Rabbi" and speaks out of terror. The voice says, "This is my dearly loved Son. Listen to him!" (Mark 9:7), just after Peter has refused Jesus' talk of suffering. Coming down, Jesus orders silence until he has risen (Mark 9:9). The churches differ on the nature of the light the disciples saw; see the card on Mark 9.

sections.h: Elijah on the mountain and Elijah who has come (Mark 9:4–13)
sections.b: Some people thought Jesus was Elijah (Mark 8:28). On the mountain Elijah appears with Moses and talks with Jesus (Mark 9:4). Coming down, the disciples ask why the scribes say Elijah must come first, as Malachi 4:5–6 promised. Jesus agrees that Elijah comes first and sets everything right, then says Elijah has already come and was treated as people pleased (Mark 9:11–13): John the Baptist, whose story echoes Elijah's struggle with Jezebel.

Mark does not name John in 9:13, but readers who remember John's Elijah-like clothing (Mark 1:6) and his death at the wish of Herodias (Mark 6:17–29) understand that "Elijah has in fact come" means John. Matthew 17:13 spells it out. The forerunner suffered, and so must the one he prepared for.

sections.h: "I believe! Help me with my unbelief!" (Mark 9:23–24)
sections.b: The father of the boy with a speechless spirit asks Jesus to help "if there is anything you are able to do." Jesus throws his words back: "'If you are able'? For the one who believes, anything is possible." The father answers with a prayer of mixed faith, and his son is freed (Mark 9:22–27). Earlier the Syrophoenician woman's answer wins healing for her daughter (Mark 7:29), and the disciples, who have seen two feedings, are asked whether their hearts have gone hard (Mark 8:17).

When the disciples ask why they could not throw out the spirit, Jesus answers that nothing can make this kind come out "except prayer" (Mark 9:29). Most manuscripts add "and fasting," which the oldest lack. Since Jesus does not pray aloud in the scene, many interpreters take him to mean a life of dependence on God rather than a technique.

Mark's only uses of Gehenna come in three sayings about cutting off a hand or foot and throwing out an eye that trips you up: better to enter life, or the kingdom of God, maimed than to go into Gehenna, "into the fire that cannot be put out" (Mark 9:43–47). The sayings end with Isaiah's last verse, "where their worm never dies and the fire is never put out" (Mark 9:48; Isaiah 66:24). The KJV repeats that line at 9:44 and 9:46, which the oldest manuscripts lack.

Jesus promises that some of those standing there will not die before they see the kingdom of God "arrived in power" (Mark 9:1). Readers have found the fulfillment in the transfiguration that follows, in the resurrection and Pentecost, in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, in the growth of the church, or, with Albert Schweitzer, in an expected end that did not come. Mark also speaks of entering the kingdom of God as entering life (Mark 9:43–47).

sections.b: Jesus ends his teaching in Capernaum with salt: "Keep salt in yourselves, and keep peace with one another" (Mark 9:50). In Israel salt sealed offerings and covenants (Leviticus 2:13; Numbers 18:19), and to share someone's salt meant to share his table and loyalty. Disciples who had argued over rank are told to keep what makes them a covenant people.

sections.h: Mark 7–9: from bread to the cross
sections.b: Chapters 7–9 hold the turning point of Mark. The section on bread ends with the disciples' failure to understand (Mark 8:14–21); a blind man healed in two stages (Mark 8:22–26) introduces Peter's confession and the first prediction of the passion (Mark 8:27–33). The road to Jerusalem begins, with three predictions, three misunderstandings and three lessons on following (Mark 8:31–10:45). Mark's explanations of Jewish customs (Mark 7:3–4), his Latin loanwords (Mark 7:4) and his translations of Aramaic (Mark 7:11, 34) show that he wrote for Gentile readers.
